title: Throughput benchmarking harness and methodology - WIP 13
content:
Purpose
This is a working document describing the throughput benchmarking harness and recommended methodology for the serving runtime. Goal: provide repeatable, comparable, and actionable throughput numbers that reflect steady-state performance for production-like LLM workloads. Not intended to be a micro-optimisation playbook for a single PR — rather a baseline protocol for team-wide benchmarking and performance comparisons across model variants, hardware, and runtime changes.

Scope
- Throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec) as the primary metric, with secondary metrics: median/99th latency, GPU utilization, host CPU load, memory usage, and power when available.
- Workloads: text generation (causal transformers) with KV-cache enabled, typical sequence-length distributions, and batched/streaming modes.
- Components: client load generator, harness runner (orchestration), metric collector, and post-processing/analysis.

High-level methodology
1) Environment capture
   - Pin software: runtime commit hash, CUDA/cuDNN/CUDA toolkit, driver version, OS kernel, Python version, Docker image tag. Record these in the run metadata.
   - Pin model: model name + exact file checksum / artifact digest. If quantized or compiled, record the build/config used.
   - Hardware: instance type, GPU model, GPU firmware, CPU type, NUMA layout.
   - Capture environment as a single JSON blob in artifacts (we write a small env-capture script).

2) Warmup phase
   Warmup is critical: transformer runtimes have JIT/kernel warmups, cuBLAS/cudnn workspace allocation, and KV cache effects. Protocol:
   - Cold start: perform an initial cold-run set to exercise graph compilation and first-time allocations, but exclude from measurements.
   - Warmup runs: run N_warm = 3 warmup epochs of M requests (configurable; default M = 200 requests) with the target concurrency and batch-size. Use the same prompt distribution as the main test.
   - KV-cache warmup: for workloads using KV-cache across tokens (e.g., multi-turn or long prefixes), ensure warmup sequences reflect average prefix lengths so the cache warming resembles production.
   - GPU stabilisation: wait for thermal/power/stable-frequency state after warmup (sleep 5–10s and verify GPU clocks if available).

3) Steady-state measurement
   - Measurement window: choose an epoch length large enough to average micro-variability (default 300s). For short tests use at least 60s.
   - Sampling cadence: poll GPU metrics (utilization, memory) at 1s resolution, latency histograms from the server with at least 5ms resolution where possible.
   - Repeat runs: run R repeats (default R = 5) of the full measurement window. Between runs, allow a cooldown of 10s and re-check clocks. Report mean and standard deviation across runs.

4) Load generator configuration
   - Determinism: use fixed RNG seeds for any synthetic prompt selection or randomized tokenization to improve repeatability. Record the seed.
   - Workload distribution: provide exact distribution for sequence lengths (e.g., 60% short(<=32), 30% medium(512), 10% long(2048)) and token-generation stopping criteria.
   - Arrival pattern: support closed-loop (saturation/concurrency-driven) and open-loop (fixed arrival rate) modes. For throughput targets use closed-loop to ensure the server is saturated; for latency SLO tests use open-loop to maintain target QPS.
   - Concurrency vs batch-size sweep: systematically sweep concurrency values and accumulated batch sizes. For each configuration, measure time to steady-state and throughput.
   - Example loadgen flags (pseudo-command):
       ./loadgen --model-endpoint $URL --mode closed --concurrency 16 --batch-size 8 --seq-dist config/seq-dist.json --seed 42 --duration 300 --warmup 200

5) Measurement artifacts and metrics
   - Primary: tokens/sec (combined across all GPUs), requests/sec, effective batch size distribution.
   - Latency percentiles: p50, p90, p95, p99, and max. Report both per-request and per-token (for generation workloads).
   - Resource metrics: GPU utilization, GPU memory, host CPU util, NIC bandwidth.
   - Derived: tokens per GPU-second, tokens per watt (if power metrics exist), and cost-per-token (unit cost estimates).

6) Repeatability checklist (for each test run)
   - [ ] Env capture file present and stored with run artifacts
   - [ ] Model artifact checksum recorded
   - [ ] Loadgen seed and config stored (including seq-dist file)
   - [ ] Warmup completed and logs saved
   - [ ] R >= 3 runs completed for this config
   - [ ] No intervening system changes (driver reloads, CRIU, docker updates)

Load generator details and recommended tools
- We support an internal ‘loadgen’ (go-based) and wrappers for vegeta/wrk for simple request-level tests. Internal loadgen supports sequence distributions, streaming tokens capture, and KV-cache-aware sessions.
- Key features to use: fixed seeds, session stickiness (for KV-cache scenarios), controlled request pacing, multiple clients to saturate network path, and per-client metrics.

Load profiles and sample sequence distributions
- Small chat messages: mean tokens/input 32, generation length 16, steering tokens 8.
- Long prompts: mean tokens/input 1024, generation length 512.
- Mixed-production: 70% small, 20% medium (<=512), 10% long (1024+).
- Provide the seq-dist as JSON file checked into benchmarks repo and referenced by checksum.

Statistical handling and reporting
- Report mean and 95% confidence intervals across repeat runs (use t-distribution unless >30 runs).
- Highlight any run with >5% deviation from median as an outlier; keep but flag it and include investigation notes.
- For comparing changes (A/B) run paired experiments when possible (same machine, back-to-back), and report paired t-test p-values and effect sizes.

Profiling and bottleneck identification guidance
- If throughput doesn't scale with increased concurrency, inspect: GPU occupancy, kernel fusion regressions, host-side bottlenecks (data prep/IO), and PCIe saturation.
- Use nvprof/nsys for kernel timelines; capture at least one trace per configuration (during steady-state).
- Capture host flamegraphs for the Python/inference server process to find serialization or tokenization hotspots.
- Check memory allocator logs (tc-malloc/ptmalloc) when seeing CPU stalls.
- For batching path regressions, keep a variant of tests with batch-size=1 to isolate batching-effects.

Common pitfalls and mitigations
- Non-deterministic prompt ordering: make prompt order deterministic or record the full request log for replays.
- Background daemons: ephemeral monitoring agents can perturb results; run tests on minimally provisioned images and note any background services.
- Thermal throttling: GPU clocks can vary; pin clocks if investigating micro-changes or at least record clock frequencies.
- Cache effects: filesystem caches and model artifact caches (mmap) can change cold-starts; always exclude cold-start from steady-state metrics.

Artifacts to store with each benchmark run
- env-capture.json, loadgen-config.json, seq-dist.json, model-checksum.txt, runtime-commit.txt, per-run metric CSVs, nsys trace files, loadgen raw logs, and a short run-summary.txt with run parameters and observed summary metrics.

Recommended baseline configs (starting points)
- Small-model (<=6B) baseline: concurrency sweep [8,16,32], batch-size sweep [1,4,8], measurement 300s, repeats 5.
- Large-model (>=70B) baseline: concurrency [1,2,4], batch-size [1,2,4], measurement 300s, repeats 5, warmup 500 requests.

Next steps and open questions
- Automate run submission in CI with guardrails: nightly benchmark runs on a stable infra lane and PR-triggered quick smoke tests.
- Explore statistical bootstrapping for tighter CIs on small-run budgets.
- Define cost-model mapping from tokens/sec to expected cloud costs for Dedicated sizing recommendations.

Appendix: example seq-dist.json (human-readable)
{
  "buckets": [
    {"max_tokens": 32, "prob": 0.7},
    {"max_tokens": 512, "prob": 0.2},
    {"max_tokens": 2048, "prob": 0.1}
  ],
  "generation_mean": 16
}

Notes to reviewers
- This is a work-in-progress; primary goal is to converge on a stable, minimal set of required artifacts so that benchmarking is reproducible across teams. Feedback particularly welcomed on: default warmup sizes, repeat counts, and what to include in env-capture.

Quick references
